Unofficial until approved by the
  Alhambra City Council

  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  May 12, 2025
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:06 p.m., on Monday, May 12, 2025, the Alhambra City Council met in the Council
Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  MAZA, MALONEY, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager
Hembree, City Attorney Montes, City Clerk Myles, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director
of Finance Lieu, Director of Community Development Ho, Principal Planner McCurley, Director of
Public Works and Utilities Ahlen, Chief of Police Kennedy, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Director
of Library Services LohGuan, Director of Human Resources Ko, Manager Analyst Alvarez, Public
Information Specialist Rodriguez

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Lee

LEE: Mayor Lee read the City’s Mission Statement as follows: The City of Alhambra is dedicated to
responsive, creative leadership and quality services, ensuring desirable neighborhoods and a
supportive business environment, while being sensitive to the diversity of our community.

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize
respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples throughout California,
especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with respect and gratitude for the
Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their
examples that we are reminded of our greater responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take
care of each other.

CEREMONIALS

1.  PROCLAMATIONS – F2M25-3

  A.  The Alhambra City Council ratified the action of Mayor Lee in proclaiming May 2025
  as Asian American Native Hawaiian Pacific Islander Heritage Month in Alhambra.

  B.  The Alhambra City Council ratified the action of Mayor Lee in proclaiming June 2025
  as LGBTQ+ Pride Month in Alhambra.

2.  COMMENDATION: MATTHEW WONG – EDISON SCHOLAR – F2M25-3

  Mayor Lee and the Alhambra City Council wished to congratulate and commend Matthew
  Wong upon receiving a $50,000 scholarship from Southern California Edison due to his
  excellence in STEM-related fields and his pursuit of a career in sustainability and innovation.
  Mr. Wong, a student at Mark Keppel High School and a former City of Alhambra Building &
  Safety Department summer intern, would attend Stanford University in the fall. Mr. Wong
  aimed to improve earthquake safety using his Computer Science and Geophysics degrees to
  1
5-12-25
   create modeling of ground motion during seismic events in order to help in the design of safer
  buildings, to prevent retrofitted structures from collapsing and to improve building plans. The
  City of Alhambra was pleased to congratulate Mr. Wong for his academic achievements and
  offered very best wishes for success in his future endeavors. Mayor Lee and a representative
  from Southern California Edison recognized Mr. Wong, who was absent.

3.  COMMENDATIONS: FREMONT & NORTHRUP ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS DUAL
  IMMERSION PROGRAM STUDENTS – F2M25-3

  Mayor Lee and the Alhambra City Council wished to recognize and commended the 8th Grade
  Spanish and Mandarin Dual Immersion Students at Fremont and Northrup Elementary
  Schools upon the occasion of their completion of the Dual Immersion Program. The Dual
  Immersion Program educates students in both English and either Spanish or Mandarin to
  encourage biliteracy and the exploration of different cultures. The City of Alhambra
  commended the teachers and students participating in the Fremont Elementary and Northrup
  Elementary Dual Immersion Programs for their commitment and dedication to academic
  enrichment through bilingualism. Mayor Lee presented the commendations to the participating
  students.

  School District Board Member Kaysa Moreno, Assistant Superintendent Janet Lees, and

program for their hard work.

  Mayor LEE spoke regarding her experience learning Spanish as a teacher as well as her own
  fluency in Mandarin. She discussed the importance of learning multiple languages,
  congratulated the students for their achievement, and encouraged them to continue practicing
  their languages.
  2
5-12-25
   Councilmember WANG congratulated the students and expressed her pride for the first
  graduates of the Dual Immersion Language Program. She spoke to the benefits of the program
  from not only learning another language, but also a new way of thinking from understanding
  cultural sensitivity. She thanked the parents and teachers in the audience as well as AUSD for
  supporting this new program.

PUBLIC COMMENT FOR NON-AGENDIZED ITEMS – F2M25-4
1) Rose DARENSBOURS, 2420 Capetown Ave., spoke regarding stop signs at Hellman, Ross, and
  Westmont. She requested flashing stop signs or better signage to assist drivers in safely proceeding
  through the intersection. She also stated that the street lights on Hellman were inconsistent and needed
  to be checked.
  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER requested that Ms. Darensbours speak with the Director of
  Public Works during the meeting.

2) Elsa GUTIERREZ-AVILES, 3401 Julep Place., spoke regarding traffic issues in the Alhambra Hills
  neighborhood. She echoed Ms. Darensbours’ comments regarding traffic issues and also spoke
  regarding the increased traffic in proximity to the Interstate 10 freeway and the negative impact on the
  neighborhood.

3) Lola ARMENDARIZ requested all ceremonials be presented at a separate event rather than on the
  same agenda as a regular City Council meeting. She discussed her attendance at the Parks and
  Recreation Commission meeting in October. She requested a flag or banner be placed at the different
  aspects of the Veteran’s Memorial at Alhambra Park such as the rock and the low wall with the quote
  from Thomas Jefferson.

4) Sawyer BROOKS, 118 E. McLean St., spoke regarding the protection of immigrant communities within
  Alhambra and the threat to them under the Trump presidential administration. He requested that
  Council codify the Alhambra Police Department policy to not assist ICE into law. He also requested a
  legal defense fund, rights education, multi-language outreach, cross agency protections, and
  connection with other cities in the San Gabriel Valley. He also requested that the Alhambra Police
  continue to protect the community.

5) Lahiru MODITUWAHLEN, representing Community Health Alliance, spoke regarding second-hand
  smoke in Multi-Unit Housing. He distributed a handout to Council, which is on file in the City Clerk’s
  office. He requested Alhambra consider smoking ordinances for multi-unit housing developments and
  invited the public to the organization’s next event.

6)  Melissa MICHELSON, via Zoom, urged the public and Council to contact Assemblymember Mike
  Fong’s office regarding censorship in the classroom and teacher’s rights under AB715.

PUBLIC HEARINGS

4.  PUBLIC WORKS MAINTENANCE & IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT FISCAL YEAR 2025-2026
  RENEWAL – F2M25-33, N2M25-50, R2M25-22

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M25-50 for the City Council to hold a public
  hearing to consider the following:

  A.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone A includes the
  downtown area only and was established to provide a source of funding to operate
  and maintain specialized improvements. Those improvements included items such as
  decorative sidewalk planters, landscape medians, decorative sidewalk and paving and
  the Washington Twin streetlights. This assessment was proposed to be unchanged
  from the 2024-25 level; and,
  3
5-12-25
   B.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone B was
  established to fund debt service on a bond issue and ongoing maintenance and
  operation of the City’s streetlights, sidewalks, curb and gutters, streets, street trees,
  median landscaping and municipal parking lots and structures. The work was
  performed by a combination of a concrete crew, a two-person electrical crew (who also
  maintain traffic signals), an asphalt crew, and contractors. This assessment was
  proposed to be unchanged from the 2024-25 level; and,

  C.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone C was
  established in 1987 and includes generally those properties located on both sides of
  Main Street, between Atlantic and Palm, and on both sides of Palm, between Main
  and Commonwealth. The purpose of Zone C was to provide funding for the ongoing
  maintenance and operation of the public improvements, which were constructed in the
  Auto Row area and include the grass parkway, the feature lights between Atlantic and
  Olive, and the street trees. This assessment was proposed to be unchanged from the
  2024-25 level.

  Director of Public Works and Utilities AHLEN delivered a staff report.

  Opened & Closed the Public Hearing: Mayor LEE opened the public hearing and as there
  was no one present who wished to speak, closed the same.

  Discussion: Councilmember WANG discussed the remaining balance for the Public Works
  Maintenance District with City Manager BINNQUIST and City Attorney MONTES. Ms. WANG
  requested staff explore the use of a portion of the fund for the Streetlight Master Plan.
  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. AHLEN discussed Zone B and the residential
  properties in it. Mayor LEE, Ms. WANG, and Ms. BINNQUIST further discussed the remaining
  fund balance which could be used for the Street Light Master Plan.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M25-22 entitled:  A
  Resolution of the Alhambra City Council ordering the renewal of the City of Alhambra Public
  Works Maintenance and Improvements District No. 1 for Fiscal Year 2025-2026 confirming
  the Assessment Diagram and Assessment therefor and providing for the Assessment Levy in
  connection therewith renewing the Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District for
  the 2025-26 Fiscal year at the same rates since 1996-97; and, directed staff to undertake the
  steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

5.  PUBLIC HEARING FOR THE COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT BLOCK GRANT (CDBG) AND
  HOME FUNDS 2025- 2029 CONSOLIDATED PLAN, 2025-2026 ANNUAL ACTION PLAN,
  AND ANALYSIS OF IMPEDIMENTS TO FAIR HOUSING CHOICE (AI) – F2M25-36,
  N2M25-40, M2M25-70

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M25-40 for the City Council to hold a public
  hearing regarding Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME funding for the
  City of Alhambra’s proposed 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan to receive
  comment pursuant to and in compliance with the Federal Department of Housing and Urban
  Development (HUD) pre-submission requirements as outlined in section 24 Part 91 of the
  Code of Federal Regulations. Management Analyst ALVAREZ delivered a staff report. For FY
  2025–2026, while HUD had not officially notified the City of its funding allocations, the City
  4
5-12-25
   could proceed with the hearing of its Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan. Using an
  estimated funding amount based on the FY 2024–2025 CDBG and HOME allocations, the
  City of Alhambra anticipated receiving approximately $834,539 in CDBG funds and $440,224
  in HOME funds from HUD. If the actual FY 2025-2026 allocations for CDBG or HOME were
  greater or less than the estimates used, the amount for each project would be increased or
  decreased at the same percentage, with Admin, CHDO Reserve, and Public Services amounts
  (as applicable) rounded down to the nearest dollar to remain under the funding caps. The
  following programs were proposed for funding through CDBG and HOME during FY 2025-
  2026:

  Proposed Work Program (CDBG)  $834,539
  Administration  $141,908
  Fair Housing Services  $25,000
  Housing Rehabilitation  $342,450
  Code Enforcement  $200,000
  Public Services (Senior Case
  $125,181
  Management)

  Proposed Work Program (HOME)  $440,224
  Administration  $44,022
  CHDO (New Construction)  $66,034
  Housing Rehabilitation  $330,168

  The HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee was expected to review the Five-Year Consolidated
  Plan, the One-Year Annual Action Plan, and the Analysis of Impediments to Fair Housing
  Choice (AI), however, a quorum with the HCDA could not be secured for the regularly
  scheduled meetings of April 1, 2025, and May 6, 2025, or for a Special Meeting of the HCDA
  on May 7, 2025. As a result, individual feedback from committee members was encouraged.
  One comment was received. The notice for this hearing and the 30-day public review period
  for the 2025–2029 Consolidated Plan, 2025–2026 Annual Action Plan, and Analysis of
  Impediments to Fair Housing Choice (AI) were published in the Pasadena Star-News, La
  Opinion, and World Journal newspapers. The documents were made available for review at
  City Hall, the Library, and on the City’s CDBG Program Administration website. The public
  comment period was conducted from April 11, 2025 to May 12, 2025. As of the date of drafting
  this report, no public comments were received.

  Open Public Hearing: Mayor LEE opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:  Lewis McCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., distributed staff reports from
  previous City Council agendas and discussed the allocation process from HUD. He further
  discussed the HOME and CDBG allocations which were affected by recent federal policies.
  Mr. McCammon further discussed the recommendations in the staff report. He suggested
  using the majority of funding for housing projects.

  Closed Public Hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor LEE closed the public
  hearing.

  Discussion: Vice Mayor MALONEY and Mr. ALVAREZ discussed Mr. McCammon’s
  comments and suggestions. Mr. ALVAREZ clarified the priority levels with HUD.
  Councilmember WANG and Mr. ALVAREZ discussed the estimated funding allocation and
  receiving anticipated funds. Ms. WANG and Mr. ALVAREZ went on to discuss funding
  timelines.

  5
5-12-25
   Action Taken:  After receiving public testimony, the Mayor closed the public hearing
  and the City Council approved the proposed FY 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, FY 2025-2026
  Annual Action Plan, and Analysis of Impediments to Fair Housing Choice (AI) for the
  Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME programs, and authorized staff to
  submit these plans to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).
  (M2M25-70)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: WANG
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

6.  CITY VACANCIES, RECRUITMENT AND RETENTION EFFORTS  REPORT  IN
  COMPLIANCE WITH ASSEMBLY BILL 2561 – F2M25-2, M2M25-69

  Director of Human Resources KO delivered a staff report. Effective January 1, 2025, Assembly
  Bill 2561 added California Government Code Section 3502.3 which required public agencies
  to hold a public hearing at least once per fiscal year to report on vacancy and recruitment
  status and retention efforts. The public hearing presentation must be made prior to the
  adoption of the final budget for the fiscal year. The City had 411 full-time positions budgeted
  with 20 of these positions vacant as of April 29, 2025, for an approximately 4.9% vacancy
  rate. A summary table showing the number of vacancies and percentage of total vacancies by
  each City bargaining unit and other unrepresented units was available as a part of the Director
  of Human Resources & Risk Management’s May 12, 2025 staff report. AB 2561 further
  required that recognized bargaining units be allowed to speak and/or make a presentation
  before the City Council during the same public hearing in which the agency makes its annual
  presentation on vacancies. All of the City’s represented bargaining units were notified of this
  public hearing tonight and provided with their vacancy rate. AB 2561 also required that during
  the hearing, the agency must identify any necessary changes to policies, procedures, and
  recruitment activities that may lead to hiring obstacles. Staff had not identified any necessary
  changes to policies and procedures that may present obstacles in the hiring process; rather,
  staff identified an opportunity to allow eligible part-time/hourly employees the ability to apply
  for promotional opportunities by amending the Alhambra Municipal Code. Additionally, within
  the past 18 months, City staff adopted various strategies to address recruitment challenges
  and improve employee retention. Efforts included updating class specifications to ensure job
  requirements are current and necessary; streamlining the hiring process for safety sensitive
  positions; reaching agreement with certain bargaining units to allow for a certain number of
  “overhires” for vital safety sensitive positions to ensure a smooth transition of personnel with
  impending retirements; adjusting work schedules for more efficient operations and employee
  wellness; and the offering of lateral hiring bonuses for Police Officers, Firefighter/Paramedics
  and Police Dispatchers.

  Opened & Closed the Public Hearing: Mayor LEE opened the public hearing and as there
  was no one present who wished to speak, closed the same.

  Discussion:  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Vice Mayor MALONEY supported
  the item.

  Action taken:  City Council conducted a public hearing and received and filed the
  information presented on position vacancies in compliance with Assembly Bill 2561 (AB 2561)
  - Local public employees; vacant positions. (M2M25-69)

5-12-25
   Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE

PRESENTATIONS

7.  APPROVAL OF TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES POLICY – F2M24-33, M2M25-76

  Director of Public Works and Utilities AHLEN delivered a staff report. On April 14, 2025, the
  City Council received a presentation and information regarding a Traffic Calming Guidelines
  and Speed Humps Policy, and directed staff to make revisions to the policy. Staff will present
  information regarding the revisions and changes to the updated Traffic Calming Guidelines
  Policy. Staff attempted to hold a special meeting of the Transportation Commission on April
  30, 2025 for their review and comments of the draft Traffic Calming Guidelines, per Council’s
  direction, but there was not a quorum to hold the meeting, thus the policy was redirected to
  City Council for consideration. The Traffic Calming Guidelines Policy documents were outlined
  in Director of Public Works & Utilities’ May 12, 2025 staff report.

  Public Comment:
  1) Henry AVILES, 3401 Julip Pl., shared concerns regarding speed humps, speed cushions, and
  rumble strips as level 3 traffic calming measures given that they were not recommended in the
  California Manual on Uniform Control Devices. He suggested that these devices should be
  considered as stand-alone devices by City Council and that they should be installed by City
  ordinance. He went on to express concerns regarding the different levels of traffic control
  devices, the petition process, and cited specific sections which he felt should be addressed.

  2) Lola ARMENDARIZ suggested that Council continue the item until the policy could be properly
  reviewed by the Transportation Commission as the previous meeting was canceled due to a
  lack of quorum. She went on to request additional Council study session meetings to gain
  additional input from the public. She further discussed the revisions made to the policy which
  she did not have time to review. Ms. Armendariz expressed concerns regarding the
  Transportation Commissioner’s not attending meetings, use of speed humps and the negative
  impact on traffic, lack of signage to warn drivers of changes to the road, the installation of bike
  lanes, and raised sidewalks. She requested additional time for public comment on non-
  agendized items.

  3) Jennifer NG, S. Cordova St., echoed Ms. Armendariz’s comments and expressed frustration at
  the lack of quorum at the last Transportation Commission meeting. She shared concerns
  voiced by other members of the public such as reviewing accident records during the
  assessment period, negative impact on parked cars in her neighborhood due to traffic issues,
  and methods for conducting traffic counts. She suggested the policy consider changing narrow
  streets to one-way traffic.

  4) Lewis McCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., reviewed concerns from public comments made at
  previous City Council meetings and the changes to the policy.

  5) Marie LOPEZ, 2821 Poplar Blvd., echoed comments expressing concerns regarding the
  cancelled Transportation Commission meeting. She further expressed concerns regarding the
  generic nature of the policy which did not consider the unique traffic conditions in various
  neighborhoods in Alhambra. She further discussed the traffic conditions in her neighborhood
  and the lack of adequate traffic devices implemented by the City. She requested additional
  means for receiving input from residents regarding traffic conditions.

  6)  Gina GARCIA, via Zoom, thanked Council for the updates made to the policy but expressed
  concerns regarding the lack of an appeal process. She discussed the appeal process used by
  7
5-12-25
   neighboring cities, the difficulty of residents going through the process, the need for input from
  the Transportation Commission, questioned the restrictions placed on wider residential streets,
  and questioned the timeframe to request a removal of traffic devices.

  7)  Melissa MICHELSON, via Zoom, supported a robust democratic process driven by data to
  review traffic calming devices in different neighborhoods. She supported the comments of
  previous speakers. She discussed the contract with the Chamber of Commerce which was
  approved at a previous meeting and suggested reviewing the cost of the contract in favor of
  providing additional funds for traffic measures.

  8)  Diane L., via Zoom, suggested that streets with higher complaint volume be given budgetary
  priority in terms of allocating traffic calming measures. She questioned terms such as
  “reasonable tolerances” or “profile defamation” should be reconsidered in favor of more
  technical standards or measurable criteria for staff to use. She agreed with Ms. Garcia’s
  comments regarding an appeal process for residents and suggested that the Transportation
  Commission be required to become more actively involved in the creation of the policy and
  budget allocation for traffic calming measures. She emphasized the need to continue the
  consideration of pedestrian safety and wellness over the convenience of cars.

  Discussion:  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed public comment
  from Ms. Lopez regarding the use of existing data and complaints for specific streets to help
  address concerns, suggested a separate ordinance to dictate use of speed humps since they
  were not included in the California Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), and
  suggested use of Measure R funds for traffic calming devices. She further suggested
  continuing to seek public engagement and input from the Transportation Commission. She
  also requested clarification regarding staff response time for each case. Ms. ANDRADE-
  STADLER also commented on the need for more Police staff in the Traffic Division to support
  enforcement of existing traffic laws.

  Vice Mayor MALONEY supported the changes made to the policy and discussed several
  points for which he wanted further clarification such as the review process for eligibility, the
  petition process, width limit of streets, and the definition of local road versus residential street
  to determine speed limits. City Manager BINNQUIST provided clarification regarding
  procedures and Bahman JANKA, Principal Traffic & Transportation Engineer with Transtech
  Engineers, provided clarification regarding other technical aspects. Mr. JANKA continued to
  discuss how the MUTCD would provide traffic engineers the guidelines for eligibility of speed
  hump installation but not the design levels which would be set by Council. Mr. JANKA and Mr.
  MALONEY discussed the critical speed threshold criteria and the concerns of the public that
  the 85% cited was too high on residential streets. Mr. MALONEY discussed his suggestion to
  reduce threshold and Mr. JANKA provided clarification. They continued to discuss streets
  eligible for Level 3 after Levels 1 and 2 had been previously implemented without measurable
  improvement.

  Mr. MALONEY and City Attorney MONTES discussed the process after the policy is adopted
  and Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestion of a separate ordinance for speed humps. Ms.
  ANDRADE-STADLER clarified her concerns.

  Mr. MALONEY suggested modifying language regarding streets which have already been
  through the equivalent of Levels 1 and 2 to clarify their eligibility for Level 3. He supported
  moving forward with the guidelines to allow for budget adjustments at the next Council meeting
  for the new fiscal year budget approval. He referred to public comments regarding the lack of
  an appeal process and suggested an appeal to City Council after a denial when there was a
  question about meeting criteria. He suggested that Council could consider appeals after review
  from the Transportation Commission. He further discussed his concerns with using traffic
  accidents and collision reports as criteria for speed humps and Mr. JANKA provided
  clarification. Mr. MALONEY reiterated that he would be happy to approve the guidelines.
  8
5-12-25
   Councilmember MAZA thanked staff and the consultants for making changes requested by
  Council. He suggested reviewing the graphic design of the document, stressed the need to
  not make it overly difficult for the public to request Level 3 improvements, and supported the
  suggestion of adding an appeal process.

  Councilmember WANG commented on the community’s engagement with the document and
  stated that she appreciated their input. She offered clarification on the exclusion of speed
  humps from the MUTCD due to their classification as roadway design features and the
  engineering guidelines developed by the consultants to cover their implementation. She also
  addressed the speaker’s concerns regarding the lack of input from the Transportation
  Commission and clarified that it was Council who recommended that the Policy go back to the
  Transportation Commission for additional review but that quorum was not reached at the last
  two meetings. She stated that Council has heard the requests of the public for urgency and
  that they were trying to move quickly. She stated that she felt it did not make sense for the
  policy to go back to the Transportation Commission at this stage. Ms. WANG referred to
  clarification provided for streets which had already attempted the equivalent of lower levels
  and could now request Level 3 under the new policy. She pointed out that this addressed the
  concerns raised by Ms. Andrade-Stadler for a standalone ordinance. She added that there
  would continue to be opportunities for the public to provide more input. Ms. WANG and Mr.
  JANKA continued to discuss the differences between each Level and the intention to provide
  multiple options at Level 2 due to their cost effectiveness compared to methods used in Level
  3. Ms. WANG stressed the need to make sure the criteria was not overly stringent and that the
  different levels were in balance. She agreed with Mr. Maloney’s suggestion to provide an
  appeal process and echoed Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s comments regarding the importance of
  traffic enforcement. She also supported using Measure R dollars in city boundaries for
  improvements. Ms. WANG went on to discuss Mr. Maloney’s comments regarding the collision
  record and its part in the MUTCD guidelines. She suggested that staff pursue new standards
  to help develop guidelines which would continue the City’s shift from car-centric policies to
  people-centric policies which prioritize pedestrian safety. She stated that she was ready to
  approve the Policy.

  Mayor LEE and Mr. JANKA discussed Council’s suggestions and the changes that could be
  made based on this meeting’s discussion. Ms. LEE went on to express her concerns with the
  difficulty in requesting Level 3 changes and the lengthy timeline for requests. Mr. JANKA
  clarified the process for residents to submit requests, the evaluation period by staff and police,
  the documentation of any changes to speed, and the timeline for consideration of requests to
  upgrade from lower levels to higher levels. Ms. LEE suggested that staff intercede when they
  see that traffic conditions did not improve at lower levels. Mr. JANKA clarified the need to
  attempt lower levels first to see if issues could be resolved at lower cost mechanisms. Ms.
  LEE continued to express concerns and stated that funding should not be a barrier to the
  installation of higher-level traffic mitigation devices. She suggested that the budget for the
  potential installation of higher-level devices should be secured before the policy could be
  adopted.

  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER and Ms. WANG addressed Ms. Lee’s concerns and clarified that
  Council could discuss funding for traffic mitigation during discussion of Agenda Item No. 7 –
  2025 Strategic Plan Funding Recommendations. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER, Ms. WANG, and
  Mr. MAZA agreed with Ms. Lee’s points, but added that they supported moving forward. Mr.
  MAZA, Ms. BINNQUIST, and Mr. JANKA discussed the use of speed trailers.

  Mr. MALONEY requested further clarification regarding language on page 49. He summarized
  Council’s direction to staff to lower the critical speed threshold, allow flexibility of the 40-foot
  street width limit, clarify that certain streets could automatically be considered for Level 3
  improvements after methods the equivalent to Levels 1 and 2 have been previously attempted.
  Mr. JANKA stated that they could address all of Council’s suggestions but requested further
  9
5-12-25
   clarification regarding the 85th percentile critical speed threshold wherein 15% of the recorded
  speeds were above the speed limit. Mr. JANKA made recommendations and continued to
  discuss the critical speed threshold with Mr. MALONEY and Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER.

  Ms. LEE suggested that the policy would return to Council in a year to evaluate its efficacy.
  Ms. LEE, Mr. JANKA, and Ms. BINNQUIST continued to discuss funding, budget allocation,

25.  CONSIDERATION OF AN ORDINANCE AMENDING CHAPTER 2.48 OF THE
  ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE CONCERNING PROMOTIONAL EXAMS – F2M25-2,
  O2M25-4846

  Periodically amendments are needed to the Alhambra Municipal Code (“AMC”) based upon
  changes in legislation and issues arising in implementation of the AMC. This proposed
  ordinance made amendments to AMC subsections 2.48.030 and 2.48.090(B). The AMC
  currently prohibited part-time employees from applying for full-time promotional examinations.
  This limited the available talent pool for positions and limits opportunities for part-time
  employees to advance their careers with the City. An amendment to the two subsections cited
  was necessary to allow eligible part-time/hourly employees to apply and to provide more
  promotional opportunities for the City’s part-time/hourly employees.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council declared introduced for its first reading the following
  ordinance entitled:
  Ordinance No. O2M25-4846: An Ordinance of the Alhambra City Council
  amending Chapter 2.48 of the Alhambra Municipal Code concerning promotional
  exams

  which ordinance will return for a second reading and adoption at the next regular Council
  meeting.

COUNCIL COMMUNICATIONS (ANNOUNCEMENTS & FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS) – F2M25-7
Councilmember WANG reported on her attendance at the Southern California Association of Governments
(SCAG) General Assembly regional conference earlier in the month where they discussed regional issues
like housing, transportation, and sustainability. She stated that the general assembly approved SCAG’s
budget for the next year, elected new officers, received updates on the regional planning efforts, and how
cities could prepare for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER reported on the Alhambra High School Academic Decathlon Team’s
performance at the National competition where they placed sixth in the nation. She also stated that Mark
Keppel High School’s team ranked ninth, and a student from Alhambra High School placed second highest
in the nation. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER thanked Council for their support of the Alhambra Latino
Association and reported that she would be present at the Library to hear more about the no-smoking
policies in the City.

Plan input meetings throughout the month of May and the Annual Memorial Day Ceremony at Alhambra
Park Veteran’s Memorial.
